newsitem.title: USA: Brazil state banks must adapt to new economy - Malan.
newsitem.headline: Brazil state banks must adapt to new economy - Malan.

text.p: Brazil's state banks will need to transform themselves over the next few years to adjust to a new economy featuring stable prices and sustained growth, Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan said Saturday.
Malan, speaking at an Inter-American Development Bank panel, said the country's private banks have learned how to operate in a non-inflationary environment, but state banks needed dramatic change.
"The worst is over," Malan said. "We are confident that we will be able to handle it in an orderly way."
Under terms of a rescue plan unveiled last month, Brazil's federal government asked states to privatize, liquidate or transform the banks into development organizations.
In turn, Brasilia would assume the debts of state banks, which were heavily burdened by years of lending to free- spending political leaders.
"The process will be unfolding for the next two years." Malan said. "It doesn't pose any systemic risk."
Noting that state banks are now barred from extending loans to state enterprises, Malan said governors needed to seriously consider the future of their banks.
"The direction is clear. There is a powerful incompatibility between politics and banking," Malan said. "It's hard to imagine a bank changing ownership every four years."

An IMF report on international capital markets released 10 days ago pointed out that Brazil's banks have been under pressure since the country launched a stabilization program in 1994 after many years of living under high inflation.
The central government has placed five state banks under temporary administration, including the two largest.
Rio de Janiero's state bank Banerj is being run by a private institution in preparation for its privatization by January 1, 1997, Malan said.
"We will be able to handle the situation as we have done so far," Malan said. "It is not an imminent problem but it's something we will be handling in the next couple of years."
